content: The document titled Water, Sanitation, and Hygiene in Health Care Facilities: Practical Steps to Achieve Universal Access to Quality Care was published by the World Health Organization (WHO) in 2019. It is available in both electronic and print versions, with respective ISBNs 978-92-4-151551-1 and 978-92-4-000768-0. The publication highlights the critical importance of water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) services in health care facilities. It notes that many health care facilities worldwide lack basic WASH services, which compromises patient safety, dignity, and the quality of care. This deficiency also increases the risk of antimicrobial-resistant infections and undermines efforts to improve maternal and child health. The Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) emphasize universal health coverage, including access to WASH services, as a prerequisite for quality care. WASH is particularly vital for safe childbirth and achieving global health targets, such as WHO’s triple billion goals and UNICEF’s Every Child Alive campaign. The document outlines eight practical steps for improving and sustaining WASH services in health care facilities. These include developing national roadmaps, setting targets, improving infrastructure and maintenance, and engaging communities. It also provides case studies illustrating successful implementation of these steps in various countries. The publication serves as a companion to the WHO/UNICEF Joint Monitoring Programme’s 2019 Global Baseline Report, which provides the first national, regional, and global estimates for SDG 6, calling for universal access to WASH in households, schools, and health care facilities. The global status of WASH in health care facilities is concerning. For example, over 1 in 4 health care facilities in sub-Saharan Africa lack water services, and sanitation services are even less prevalent. Facilities in low-income countries are three times more likely to lack water services compared to those in high-income countries. Non-hospital facilities are twice as likely to lack water or sanitation services compared to hospitals. The burden of maternal sepsis is twice as high in lowand middle-income countries as in high-income countries, further underscoring the need for improved WASH services. The document sets global targets for WASH in health care facilities, aiming for 60% of facilities to have at least basic WASH services by 2022, 80% by 2025, and 100% by 2030. Higher levels of service are to be defined and monitored in countries that have already achieved universal basic WASH services, with the goal of achieving these higher levels in 80% of such countries by 2030. Priority is given to facilities where births occur, as WASH improvements in these settings can have a significant impact on maternal and neonatal health. The publication concludes by calling for greater leadership, investment, and accountability to ensure universal access to WASH services in health care facilities. It emphasizes that this is a solvable problem with a high return on investment and seeks the support of governments, partners, and stakeholders to achieve this critical goal.
